question.prompt:
In the figure, \(ABCD\) is an isosceles trapezoid with side lengths \(AD=BC=5,\) \(AB=4,\) and \(DC=10.\) The point \(C\) is on \(\overline{DF}\) and \(B\) is the midpoint of hypotenuse \(\overline{DE}\) in the right triangle \(DEF.\) Then \(CF=\)

[Figure 1](figures/1989_AMC_12_Q04_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The equal legs of the trapezoid let us split the difference between its bases equally. Then the midpoint condition connects that information to the larger right triangle.

[Figure 1](figures/1989_AMC_12_Q04_question_fig1.svg)

Draw perpendiculars from \(A\) and \(B\) to \(DC\), with feet \(P\) and \(Q\), respectively. Since \(AB\parallel DC\), the quadrilateral \(ABQP\) is a rectangle. Thus \(PQ=AB=4\) and \(AP=BQ\).

The right triangles \(DAP\) and \(CBQ\) have equal hypotenuses \(AD=BC=5\) and equal legs \(AP=BQ\). They are therefore congruent by the hypotenuse-leg criterion, giving \(DP=CQ\). The excess length of the longer base splits between these two equal segments:
\[
DP=CQ=\frac{DC-PQ}{2}=\frac{10-4}{2}=3.
\]
Hence
\[
DQ=DC-CQ=10-3=7.
\]
Because \(DE\) is the hypotenuse of right triangle \(DEF\), the right angle is at \(F\). Thus \(EF\perp DF\), so \(BQ\parallel EF\). Since \(B\) is the midpoint of \(DE\), this parallel line meets \(DF\) at its midpoint. To see why, let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(DF\). The triangle midpoint theorem gives \(BM\parallel EF\); the unique parallel through \(B\) is \(BQ\), so \(M=Q\).

It follows that \(DF=2DQ=14\). Since \(C\) lies between \(D\) and \(F\),
\[
CF=DF-DC=14-10=\boxed{4.0},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Use perpendicular feet and the midpoint condition
